ROUTEMEMO:
Source Peace Climb News - May 23, 1990

After weeks of battling miserable weather and high winds, dealing with illness and injuries, repairing and replacing equipment -- plus Jim and Ray's encounter with the democratic revolution in Kathmandu, no one on the mountain would say it was easy. "It just shows what can be accomplished through international cooperation and teamwork," said Whittaker. "We had horrible conditions our first two months on the mountain. A lesser team would have been stopped. But we hung in there, got the routes and the camps in and carried up supplies. So we were in position to take advantage of the break when it finally came."

The first summit group of six climbers left C6 on May 5 under less than ideal conditions: snow and wind. Lower on the mountain, it was snowing so hard that no one made carries to C4. But the next day, May 6th, dawned calm: it was one of the few windless days since the team had arrived at the Base Camp. Two Soviets (Grigory Luniakov and Sergei Arsentiev), two Chinese.

Da Cheme, Gyal Bu and two Americans (Robert Link and Steve Gall) left C7 at daybreak, negotiated the difficult "Second Step" and set foot on the summit at 1:13 pm Beijing time.

The first summit team descended through C6, some spending the night at C5, some at C4 and some at C3. Unbelievably, the weather held for another day, and before dawn on May 7, six more climbers left C6. Three of them (Ed Viesturs, Andrei Tselischev and Mistislav Gorbenko) climbed all the way to the summit, leapfrogging C7, and then descended to C6 - a feat never before accomplished on this route. And Viesturs and Tselischev managed it without the used of bottled oxygen.

The second three (Ian Wade, Gui Sang and Da Qoing) spent the night at C7 and ascended to the summit on May 8. They were joined there by two more climbers, Ren Na and Luo Tse, who had started the ascent that day from C6. On the radio from the summit, Ian Wade yelled, "I'm on top! I feel fine! Now I want to get off here."

On May 9, Jim reported from BC, "It is the most beautiful day yet. The sun is shining and the mountain looks spectacular. Seven more climbers are heading up from C6 (Mark Tucker, Ekaterina Ivanova, Anatoly Mochnikov, Ervand Ilyinsky, Alexander Tokarev, Wang Ja, and Jia Tsuo). It looks like they have a good shot if the weather holds." A few hours later, he called with the extraordinary news: "Six of the seven made it to the top - twenty climbers in all, over a four day period: the most ever to reach the summit on a single expedition!" Jia Tsuo descended because of frostbitten toes. He is expected to recover fully. But all the rest made the peak and descended without major problems.


Climb Progress Report:

Here is the itinerary followed by the Peace Climb from May 1 through May 16.

May 2  First day of good weather! First summit teams move to C5, second 
       group moves to C4. Jim and Ian carry loads to C4. Hanging from
       fixed rope, Jim is patched in by radio to Port Townsend HQ..live!
       Trekkers return to Base
May 4  Heavy snow and gusty winds at C3 and C4. First team moves to C6, 
       second to C5. Mark Tucker and Tim O'Brien carry from C4 to C5 and
       experience winds of 70 mph. They are airborne several times on
       the fixed line - they cache the loads and return to C4. Tuck
       returns to C3 to rest. Trekkers leave for Kathmandu.
May 5  Weather calm above Base. First team moves to C7, other teams 
       behind with one day separations. High avalanche danger between C3
       and C4 - no one moves on that route.
May 6  No wind! By 9:30 pm (Seattle time), the Peace Climb has 6 
       climbers on the summit. Port Townsend BC gets call from BC,
       patched to Jim at C3, then to Robert on the summit.
May 7  Three more climbers reach the summit by 9:00 pm (Seattle time). 
       Viesturs and Andrei do it without oxygen from C6 -- the first
       time anyone had gone from C6 to the summit and back on this route
       Robert and Steve down from C5 to C3, Da Cheme and Gyal Bu down
       from C3 to Base. All summit teams progress up the mountain,
       separated by one camp. Jim goes back to BC.
May 8  Third summit group puts five more on top! Gui Sang is the second 
       Chinese woman to reach the summit of Everest.
May 9  It's getting crowded at C6. Some coming down and a new team going
       up. A cloud cap on the summit, but no plume which means no wind. 
       At 7:00 pm (Seattle time) six more are on top, for a total of 
       twenty! Jim is "stunned" at this spectacular success. Ekaterina 
       is the first Soviet woman on the summit of Everest, and she 
       records a message to the women of the world. Jia Tsuo turns
       around below the summit with frostbitten feet and returns to C3
       where he receives treatment. On the way down the mountain, Ian
       Wilde suffers snowblindness and is treated by Dr. Kurt Papenfus at C4.
May 10 All summit climbers descend, cleaning up garbage and expedition
       gear as they move. "We've probably picked up a couple of tons of 
       trash," says Whittaker. "We brought down at least 50 old oxygen 
       cylinders from C4 alone. Maybe we'll shop some of it home and 
       auction it off to help pay the bills!" Steve and Robert arrive at
       Base and drink a Rainier Beer. Ian's eyes feel better and sight
       is returning. Patti calculates that she has 24 more meals to prepare.
May 11 Team members from Base go up to C3 to pack it up for the yaks to 
       carry out. Tuck (Mark Tucker), Ian and Toly (Anatoly) down from 
       C3 to Base. Trekkers return to Seattle.
May 12 Clean up continues. Yaks at ill.
May 13 Tuck arrives at Base, gives Patti the day off and makes pancakes
       for all -- even though his fingers are black with frostbite (no
       permanent damage). "Snowing like mad" at Base. Jim and Warren 
       negotiate with Chinese regarding final payment for in-China expenses.
May 14 LaVerne Woods returns to Seattle. She is in good spirits and
       recovering well from thrombophlebitis and pulmonary embolism.
May 15 They're smelling the barn. Port Townsend HQ jumps through hoops, 
       leaps tall buildings and walks on water to change plane 
       reservations and get the team home a week early.
May 17 5:58 pm (Seattle) Point. Townsend HQ faxes congratulatory letter
       President Bush to the entire team at BC. 6:15 pm (Seattle) Last 
       fax is transmitted from Mt. Everest Base Camp. Warren shuts down 
       communications equipment to pack up for trip home.

Everest - The end of an Apprenticeship

As Christchurch climber Rob Hall's voice boomed over the roof of the world, the 1990 Cold Water Surf Everest Challenge Expedition made the first broadcast from the summit of Everest direct into New Zealand homes.

For Hall as expedition organiser and Leader, reaching the top was culmination of three years effort which included two previous attempts on the mountain.

The summit of Everest effectively divides Chinese occupied Tibet from Nepal with snowflakes that fall on the top either ending up in the Tsang Po or the Ganges river catchments. As the three Kiwis were shaking hands, taking photographs and getting ready to dial up the New Zealand Prime Minister simply said to Gary "I USSR" handed him a postcard and asked Gary to take his pictures. Gary only had time to reply "I Kiwi" before the Soviet turned and stoped off down his ascent route, this climber was a member had already put 12 climbers on the summit over the previous ten days.

Soon after the three days New Zealanders began the descent of the South East Ridge back to their camp on the 8000m South Col they were engulfed in a storm. Unable to see properly they were forced to remove their goggles which immediately exposed them to high levels of UV radiation. Snow blindness was to severely hamper each of the climbers during the retreat to their 5700m base camp below the dreaded Khumbu Icefall. Snowblindness is a UV burn of the cornea which feels like having hot sand thrown in the eyes. It effectively means the eyes are too painfull to open.

Only twenty minutes below the summit the Kiwis met two other members of their international team who were sitll plodding upwards. Rudi Van Snick was soon to become the first Belgian to summit. He was accompanied by Apa Sherpa from Thame village only 50 kms from the base of the mountain. Unlike the other 14 support was invited as a friend and full climbing member of the team. Both Rudi and Apa were suffering from snowblindness by the time they reached the South Col just on dusk at 6 pm, a full two hours behind the New Zealanders. By now, Peter Hillary had descended to a lower camp in the Western Cwm.

The weather remained fine next day so Gary and Apa, with watery inflamed eyes, set off to grope their way downwards. Rob, as the least affected, stayed on the South Col to nurse a totally blind Rudi. They lay in the tent sucking oxygen through a mask. Meanwhile, two of the three Swedish members of Rob's team, Michael Reutersvard and Oskar Kihlborg, both 26 year old, had made their own way to the summit. As the first Swedes on the summit they look great pleasure in calling the King of Sweden on the Satellite-linked radio.

The Swedes spotted the lanky Australian climber, Tim Macartney-Snape, high above the South Col that day. Unlike their own ascent and that of the others in their team including, the New Zealanders, this Australian was travelling alone and wasn't using bottled oxygen. Everest is climbed regularly now without oxygen since Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler first proved the feat possible in 1978.

Rob Hall finally joined Peter and Gary at BC on May 13th, having had an epic job guiding the still partially blind Rudi down the steep icy Lhotse Face (one serious fall) then through the 500m Khumbu Icefall - chaotic jumble of crumbling ice towers that has claimed many lives in the past. The relief in his voice when interviewed at base camp for this story was more than noticeable. As he said "only now have I truly climbed my Everest."

Everything went perfectly - "extraordinary spell of good weather." In 8 hours from Col to top on 10th and 2 hours down to Col and BC 11 May and spent 1/2 hour on top in which time Russian member of Peace Expedition turned up at about 8:30.

Really difficult - no yak route.

6 March 84

Peking (AP) - An American team that tried to scale Mount Everest said Saturday it was a "grand adventure" even though the effort failed when supplies ran out a day's climb short of the 29,028 ft high mountain.

Members of the Ultima Thule (ultimate in human adventure) expedition from Seattle returned here Saturday and spoke with awe for the world's tallest peak and with satisfaction of the medical knowledge they gathered. The 15-man team included four doctors.

Expedition leader Tom Fitzsimmons, 34, a govt official in Washington state said lead climbers reached a high point of 28,200 ft on May 20. He said only one more day of climbing was needed to reach the summit and become the first Americans to conquer Everest's northeast ridge, in China's Tibet province, but they had to turn back because oxygen and food ran out.

Three members of team  had to be evacuated early in the expedition because of illness - including its original leader, Warren Thompson. However, the climb continued smoothly.

"We had three goals: climb safely, climb high and make the summit, and do medical research. We got two out of three." Fitzsimmons said "As a team, we lost 350 pounds."
 
Dr. Michael Wiedman, at 56 the oldest in the team, said the group's findings may benefit people who ski and vacation in mountainous areas by examining the cause of altitude sickness and the best remedy for it.

Yaks and porters helped carry research computers to tents at 21,300 ft, along with electro-encephalographs to measure brain waves and cameras to study eye-retina hemmorhaging.


From Don Goodman:

Everest Attempt. Our team included ten climbers: leader Thomas Fitzsimmons, Bob Berg, Jim Frush, Dave Hambly, Kurt Hanson, Ray Nichols, Greg Thompson, Warren Thompson, John Yaeger and me; two climbing doctors: Mike Colpitts and Anton Kakusa; four medical research doctors; Ben Blackett, Rick Foutch, Michael Wiedman and Rich Wohns; biomedical engineer Tom Clement; BC manager Phil Hawkins and photographer Art Wolfe. Three days travel by truck from Lhasa placed us at BC in the Rongbuk valley at 5100m on March 8. This was the same site as that used by the British in the 1920's, a mile from the snout of the Rongbuk Glacier. We spent several days organizing. The next two and half weeks passed quickly as we reconnoitered and established the route to C3 for 21 yaks and seven drivers to transport 4800 pounds of equipment. On March 28 the first yak caravan reached C3, a 5 day round trip along the rocky medial moraine of the East Rongbuk Glacier. Four different climbing teams rotated leads, placing 3000 ft of fixed line and 20 ft of rigid aluminium ladders over the steeper sections to reach the North Col. The task was completed on April 12 so that our six Tibetan porters were restricted by the Chinese Mountaineering Association to carrying only to C4, the difficult task of transporting loads to C5 was left up to the climbing team. While climbing activity was moving at a brisk pace above BC, the medical research team was equally busy setting up and fine tuning our high-tech data gatherings and computing systems. Later the same equipment performed well at heights exceeding 21,000 ft. Camp 5 was established at 7680m on April 25. Five members transported 850 pounds of oxygen and climbing equipment over a ten-day period in early May, which took a toll on their strength. While C5 was being stocked, two climbing teams were working the route from C5 to C6 at 8230m. This was more difficult than anticipated and required 1200 ft of fixed rope. C6 was established on May 15 and occupied by Tom Fitzsimmons and Greg Thompson on May 16. While others carried supplies, these 2 worked the route from C6 to C7, hindered by high winds and steep downsloping rock slabs. C7 was occupied on May 19 at 8540m. On May 20 Fitzsimmons and Thompson made a last gasp summit attempt. Upon reaching the first rock step at 8600m they realized it was futile and made a cautious retreat, reaching the North Col late that evening. On the 21st all camps above C3 were evacuated by support personnel. As per schedule yaks arrived on May 23 to evacuate C3. All personnel and equipment were back at BC on May 25.

High point was near traditional location of C6. Had had 2 summit bids but no higher than C5 because of fierce winds.

"The thing I don't like about this crowding: the most frightening time of my life." Was standing during descent at the Hillary Step on 2 small steps and with one planted ice axe while 4 ITBP summiters came up past him, roped together but to nothing else and woman kept slipping; each Indian grabbed him for a hand hold as they went up. Kazakhs did all lead climbing, all fixing ropes and all camp pitching. Sherpas came up behind them to stock camps. Kazakhs fixed entire route from base of NE Ridge to C6. Kazakhs never touched oxygen. They climbed as separate team. Sherpas primarily supported Japanese. 4 Kazakhs pitched C6 thus in position to make summit bid and slept there 2 nights of 16th & 17th May [waiting out bad weather]; went all way down to to BC to rest before trying [again] for top; Viktor and Yuri descended US route (N Ridge-N Col) while Vladimir and Valeri went down their own NE Ridge route. By this time Japanese climbers had given up and down a bit to C4 & C5. 

Japanese started for their own summit bid: Ohmyia, Hoshi, Kokobu and 3 Sherpas to C4 & C5; only Ohmyia & Hoshi from C5 to C6 with 2 Sherpas on 22 May. Sherpas on 22nd reached C6 and next day came down US route in snow & windstorm. Japanese never reached C6, but Ohmyia bivouacked at 8300m two nights (several [150m laterally] short of C6) while Hoshi never got to C6: Kazakhs found 100m below C6 a jumar on fixed rope and ice axe standing in snow. Kazakhs had received radio message from other Japanese that no contact with Ohmyia for 24 hrs and they must be in trouble, please help. Kazakhs had reached C4 on 23rd and when distress message came through, they immediately went up, climbing all night and all next day reaching Ohmyia at his bivouac late in afternoon of 24th. Ohmyia was exhausted and irrational, wouldn't take oxygen or water they offered him, was determined to go on to summit. Kazakhs had to get Japanese on radio to insist he obey Kazakhs; he was at 8300m below jummar & ice axe, which were on west side of NE Ridge. 4 Kazakhs practically carried him up to C6, which was close, well-supplied with oxygen and food and at junction of NE & N Ridges and thus on US (normal) route for easier descent; the 5 men got to C6 about 7 pm (Nepali time - nightfall) on 24th. On 25th all 5 down to US C4 at 3:30 pm by 2 Kazakhs, 7 pm by 2 other Kazakhs & Ohmyia; at C4 used German tent and Germans & Americans were there to help. 26th down to ABC despite heavy snowfall previous night with an American (Beazari) breaking trail and Austrian couple helping Ohmyia. US & doctors cared for him at ABC. By time he had reached N Col, Ohmyia could walk; his frostbite not so severe that good hospital probably couldn't save all fingers and toes; evacuated by yak to BC. Hoshi perhaps fell or jumped down W Face of NE Ridge; Ohmyia was not searching for him.

Kazakhs brought oxygen supply and Japanese provided everything else. Kazakhs drove to Kazakh-Chinese border, took public buses to airport in China with connection to Chengdu & then Lhasa; same trip in reverse back to Alma Ata from BC.

On NE Ridge Kazakhs found a tent with 2 sleeping bags, a stove, an ice hammer, a book with Chris's name in it & a diary with May 1982 entries. They took photos of body near these items; on breast of down suit was logs with outline of a mountain & 3 letters, one of which was M; they brought down book and diary.

C4 at South Col

1st summit bid from C4 on 2 May 4 members [Kulkarni, Jacob, Patel] & Anit Sah. From C3 1st May left to S Col; one member and Sah reached col about 5 pm; other 3 at last radio contact between 3 to 4 pm said were coming slowly but were well below col. 6 pm weather getting bad and asked ITBP in C4 to check in this expedition's tent of other arrived but had not. By 8 pm weather very bad. 2nd May early morning ITBP man found body 30-40 yards short of col camp and Miss Yadav recognized it as Jacob. 2 members of this team gave oxygen and little water but then he totally collapsed. Near yellow band ITBP people descending found another man hanging on rope; almost no life appeared in him (this was Kulkarni). Patel had dug out small cave and bivouacked there, 20 minutes below yellow band) and came out "hail and hearty." Time to reach bodies but bad weather continued for a week. Jacob buried under stones at col and Kulkarni's rope cut, body fell into crevasse. Now sent half of team home because they disturbed by death. 

Made summit bid: 3 members and a press reporter. From C4 on 12th Mudarris, Sah & Nepali Nima Lama at 3:30 am with ITBP team for summit. At 11:30 am were at S Summit with ITBP party. 1 pm they reported Mudarris's oxygen finished and 2 hrs more to reach the top and he quite tired and risky for him to descend alone so Puri ordered retreat and they did bring him safely to C4 where they spent that night and all of them to C1 on 13th. Thought would make another attempt on 20th with ITBP & others, but sponsoring committee sent message to abandon climb, so they did.


Hukam Singh - 2 June 1992

I was all the time worried about Indian civilians and they did not have good communication. Their members at C4 thought Kulkarni and Sangay had turned back to C3. When Khem Raj and Miss Yadav at 7:00 am left tent to descend and found man (Jacob) lying on snow with one hand bare but mouth making some noise and eyes open, recognized 2 ITBP people and he smiled - tried to save him (he was 15m from Dutch tent). Dutch not receptive to idea of saving him: took oxygen and glucose water but he immediately died. Khem Raj and Yadav then descended to just above Geneva Spur where found Kulkarni hanging by jumar to fixed rope, face swollen, body stiff in place exposed to wind (presumably dead).

Jacob's body "buried" at Col with stoves on top - about six other bodies (Sherpas) lying there in sleeping bags.

"Very ill equipped and ill prepared," but whatever help I gave was voluntary and not because they were Indian (helped rescue NZ Sherpa badly injured in fall into crevasse and brought him out of it and carried him down when other NZ Sherpas didn't want to).
ACCIDENTS: Sah and Dorje slight frostbite

ROUTEMEMO:
C2 in Cwm (next to British)
C3 on Lhotse Face
C4 at Col.

Some boulders came down from Lhotse, but C1 was safe; no damage to tent which stayed intact 1 April-22 May (contrary to New Zealanders report to me). C4 pitched 8 April but slept in 26th April. Set up C4 20 April (1st team to pitch this camp) but could not occupy it till 1 May because of bad weather (snow and wind) and again very bad weather 2 May when Islaivilans died. Heavy snowfall from early morning so summit attack for 2 May cancelled and those in C4 descended (none had gone above C4).

2nd summit party to C4 on 9th May. Left col 4 am; 11:45 S Summit and contacted leader at C2; at 2:30 pm again contacted from bottom Hillary Step and at top [of step] 1 man's oxygen exhausted and his bottle left there; at 4:05 pm contacted and said there were on top (slow because one had no oxygen and other had little oxygen) and there did puja with Ganga water. Their descent seen from S Summit; reached C4 at 9 pm without headlamps and slept there (some moonlight through fog).

3rd summit party same people as 1st party, left C4 3:30 am 12th May, when Raj turned back at north side of S Summit because oxygen regulator and mask not working). Other 5 to summit with Mohan Singh last because his oxygen finished at Hillary Step; returned to C4 at 4 pm (Lobsang) and other 4 together at 6:30 pm.

4th Summit party: 6 members and Chhoda Tshering Sherpa (India supporting member) spent 2 nights at C3 because of changable weather, nights of 17th and 18th May, went to C4 19th; 20th blizzard and could not go up, had difficult time descending to C2.

Sher Singh, cook (Indian) who also carried some loads, coming down last ladder in icefall 200m from bottom of icefall, slipped down tilted ladder with nylon sling around his waist. 22 May he died and body on 24th May carried from BC and cremated at Dugla.

Paid royalty for 15 members; had several "support members" but Chhoda Tshering Sherpa, an Indian "from the border area" was only one to go above BC.
ACCIDENTS: Papta pulmonary edema and 2 fingers bad frostbite; Bisht 3 fingers bad frostbite; Sher Singh died in the icefall

C2 before others C2 (more protected)
C3 on kidney rock right side of pillar lower spot
C4 midway up Lambert couloir, left side of big serac which divides normal

"We are very happy on our route, only us, no problems." Had difficulty making C3: 1st problem was very wide crevasse and stonefall (which slightly injured 3 members with 2 smashed helmets) and 2nd was where to put it and had to make it on ice close to stone, very small place. Took much time to fix ropes to it and to make platforms. 

1st summit [Exposito, Hernandez, Perez Grueso, Trabdo, Vegue, Dorje Pemba Jr.] attempt without oxygen on 11th May in middle of storm which aborted attempt below C4; turned back at 7900m. 

2nd attempt with oxygen on 18th May successful: left C4 at 2:30 am in bad weather (snowing and windy and very cold), on top 11:50 am Gan, Juez, Portilla and 2 Sherpas at 12:15. Left top 1 pm in good weather following; returned to C4 5 pm in strong wind by Gan and Juez while other 3 summiters to C2 at 6:30 pm exhausted. 

3rd summit attempt on 17th planned but could not go up from C4 that day; strong wind broke tents and down to C2; this attempt by 5 members and 2 Sherpas, same people who had made 1st attempt. 18th waited to see if weather improving, but getting worse, icefall getting dangerous and climb finished.

This was the only expedition this spring to climb pillar-corridor.
ACCIDENTS: Sherpa fell in icefall and injured knee

ROUTEMEMO:
Made some attempt to climb to climb SW Face but snow situation very dangerous & some members hit by stone (one member's helmet broken & another shoulder hurt slighty & 2 fingers broken & had to stop climbing). Reached 7200m 2 members 6th April. Had already decided that face not safe and would have to change route and had moved C2, but third face to be able to say they had done so. Asked permission to change route to col route; permission refused because too many other teams already on that route, but climbed it anyway. 12th May left C4 4 am, reached top 11:45 and returned C4 2:30 pm; 2 members stayed there other 2 to C3 because Volkov's fingers slightly frostbitten. 14th May another 4 to top; left C4 4 am, on top 1 pm & C4 4 pm with 2 members desending to C2 while other two very tired & stayed at C4 where had "very little tent"; no other summit bids.


Hukum Singh - 2 June 1992

The way US and NZ told Russians to wait was "very rude." These foreigners had no authority to tell them to stall off South Col route. Looked at SW Face from C2 while Singh was there, saw there was no snow on face and they could not climb it, found it extremely hazardous. Said they had tried to climb it. After 15 April did not try it (15th Singh to C2). No Indian saw them try SW Face.

Main cause of friction with New Zealand, US and Dutch was difference in attitude between commercial teams and Russian contemptuousness of commericial climbers.

They lived in ITBP tent at C4 by agreement and used of ITBP similarly by mutual agreement.


Kefford - 1 June 1992

Russians kept renegging on all their agreements. Did maintenance of Icefall only 2 days and did not wait as they agreed for NZ and US to go ahead; agreed with their intrepreter present at BC meeting.

Russians never went onto SW Face. British saw no ladders to cross bergschrund, which would have been seen by British; saw no people on face anywhere at all except Spanish army, whom saw to C3 from Cwm.


Burleson and Athans - 29 May 1992

Athans and Burleson confident 4 Russians went to top on 14th. Athans saw them just below South Summit going up. 

Russians never set foot on face. Athans never saw any activity near face except Spanish army who were far away, to right of Pillar and others could not confuse them for everyone in center of face. Athans thinks that Jan Robertson would not necessarily know about a Russian with broken fingers.

Russians agreed to everything but didn't act on agreements. Russian did fix a considerable amount of rope on Lhotse Face tied into old ropes. Then Ball and Athans went up later putting in anchors and fixing rope more securely. Total fixed on face was 800m and Russians put in at least 500m. Fixed their own rope and Athans put in ice screws, etc.

Not aware of Russians not taking their turn maintaining Icefall.

Russians did not have understanding with ITBP and Galicians.

Russian tried to enter Dutch C3, was refused entry and went to Americans, who took him in. He had no sleeping bag or down jacket for the night, which Americans lent him - was very windy. Naar's altitude was no responsibility for other teams' personnel.

Americans angry at Russians because they were unpredictable and hard to plan around them. Furthermore they were refused permission by Tourism after US and NZ leadership wrote letters of protest because they didn't do what it was understood they'd agreed to, especially waiting as agreed until others made progress upwards, coming along behind them; could have been a language problem.

Burleson calls them liars because they agreed several times to wait and then immediately broke these agreements.
ACCIDENTS: Smirnov hurt by falling stone; 3 slight frostbite

C1 slightly beyond top of Icefall and others C1
C4 at lower slope of South Col.

No problem of crowding at BC and were weekly meetings regarding garbage. Very good cooperation amongst all expeditions except Russians who decided to change route and who went with others tents and helped themselves to food. At C3 in a storm, Russian asked to come into Dutch C3 saying he couldn't find his camp but he had no C3 (it hadn't been pitched); Dutch didn't let him in and don't know what became of him. 

BC pitched 23rd March by advance team; whole expedition in BC 2nd April. 3rd May 1st summit bid reached 8300m and dropped oxygen which was used on 12th May; this by 3 members [Naar, Oefner, Van der Meulen] and 1 got slightly frostbitten three fingers and left expedition [Van der Meulen]. 

10th May 2nd bid by 2 members [only Wesker, Nima Dorje, Nima Gombu] but got only 10m above C4; inexperienced, didn't use oxygen right, panicky because of altitude and down to BC same day. 

9th May 2 members [Naar, Oefner]  with 2 Sherpas left BC to C2; 10th in C3, 11th C4, the last to leave BC and to arrive at C4 where at least 40 people were camped in plenty of space (Russians probably slept in Spanish tent). On 12th to top going between New Zealand team member moving slowly and fixing themselves ropes fixed at Hillary Step: Dutch jumped the queue formed to scale step. Left C4 at 1 am on 12th reached S Summit at 9:30 am and main summit at 11:30 am Naar first, then Dawa, Nima and lastly Oefner; returned to C4 at 5 pm, slept there and down to C2 on 13th & BC on 14th. 

No clients (who had paid $18,000) got to top and they left disappointed.

8 May - Achterbosch demoralized by Indians in front of his tent. Ritzen had had enough (had reached 6950m). Zuidhoff was sick & demoralized. Timmermans left with Zuidhoff, her boyfriend. Van der Meulen had had enough.

Use of oxygen:
Used by all who went to C4: summit team of 12 May; Dutch member used it in 10th May sleeping in C3, on 11th climbing to C4 and sleeping there; Sherpas used it sleeping in C4; all four on 12th used it from C4 to summit and back to C4 and sleeping in C4.


Ronald Naar, Dutch Everest expedition leader - 20 May 1992

This was first successful Dutch Everest Expedition. Vos's claim to have been seen by his "Sherpa" from South Summit while Vos was on main summit (Aut 1984) could not be true because, as Naar saw for himself, main summit cannot be seen from S Summit. Ganesh Gurung told Naar in 1986 & in 1988 that he saw Vos reach bottom of Hillary Step and turn back there without going higher.

Had trouble with Sherpas not very strong, sirdar left to buy food but went home actually (25th April & returned 1st May) getting loads to col. C3 tent destroyed by wind & snow 1st May. During night 20/21 May Lovato developed pulmonary edema, at 7 am started to evacuate him: asked British to provide oxygen, 2 members & 2 Sherpas manpower; 1 member came from BC to help French & British - in icefall he was close to death & arrived BC only 9 pm & 21 May Lovato rested in British BC (2 members still in BC resting). 22 May asked for helicopter on 22 May; his edema gone but some infection; 23rd bad weather so evacuated to KTM on 24th. 1 member planned up to make summit bid (BC 11 May, arrived C2 20th) but aborted this plan when Lovato became ill.

Not only Russians climbed on other expedition's backs. Only people who came truely equipped to climb Everest was Spanish army and British. Adverse comments about siege type expeditions: Frenchman would have died if British hadn't provided 3 expensive oxygen bottles, medicines, stretcher and manpower to get him through Icefall and radio communication to BC. French leader and member only struck their heads out of tents while British extracted him from his a lot of people were topping over their egos.

One of our problems was spindrift being blown around (and almost suffocating us) when almost no wind on SW Face and Cwm was still. This expedition was first to arrive at BC, put in icefall route and handed over to others to mountain. Had also sugggested where tracks between tents should be, where toilets should be after Galicians (Quinteiro) and Dutch threw stones at each other for walking through their camps. After New Zealand's Sherpas accident, got all expedition's doctors together where scratches were, etc. On SW Face went almost straight up to shoulder. 1st real technical problems were icefall and steep ice section between C2 and C3; then Hornbein Couloir top, just when you think you are through this difficulties, there is steep rock. On 18th May Bell and Hughes got to site of C6 and stashed their tent and oxygen bottles in such strong wind they had to descend and this point never reached again. Had reached C5 on 26th April but 27th started to snow and not till 6th May were able to get back to C5 because of snow conditions and wind and to rest lower camps. Started work on Couloir on 12th. ROUTEMEMO:
C1 at North Col
C2 at North Ridge
High point at North Face in traverse from North Ridge.

No C3: tried to go to top from C2 but bad snow at 7900m and decided to put a camp at 8300m but no one could reach this altitude. From C2 on 27 Sept by Fuster, who reached 8100m and turned back with cold feet and bad snow conditions (hard cover on powdered snow) and lost too much energy and returned to ABC. 1st Oct Sala, Verzaroli and Fuster in C2 to go next day to make C3 at 8300m, but winds so strong could not go as high as 7900m and back to ABC. Stayed in ABC, tried again: same 3 got to C2, but tent broken and not possible to put another tent, so back to 7650m where Taiwanese had camp, more sheltered from wind and or Taiwanese Sherpa helped put up tent here. Stormy night and on 10th down to ABC while Giabiati stayed at this camp at 7650m; he went up on 10th to C2 to retrieve gear only.

Climbing route was from east side of col to col, up N Ridge to C2 & then across N Face towards Great Couloir.
ACCIDENTS: None except Verzaroli abcessed tooth at end

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 7600m due bad weather and lack of time
ROUTEMEMO:
C1 as same as Americans
C2 as same as Americans
C3 as same as Americans
C4 as same as Americans by Savoldelli and Poloni.

Did not attempt W Ridge because of avalanching. Used same route as Americans and had C1, C2 and C3 in place. Tried to go into couloir but deep unstable snow. 20th Sept Dalla Longa and Birolini made 1st summit bid from C3; got to 7600m but winds too strong and down to C3. 2nd summit bid from C3 on 21st by Carminati and Rota; got to C4, spent the night, during which wind got very strong and down to ABC on 22nd. Yaks arriving at ABC on 25th so no more attempts. Could probably have gotton to top if leader hadn't had to get home 1st Oct.

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 7610m due to dangerous snow conditions
ROUTEMEMO: Never attempted Great Couloir because snow conditions too dangerous with avalanches, avalanching to west of C2. First camps put in fairly rapid order - made cache at 7400m on way to making C4; winds from west stopped advance that day so dumped loads and retreated to C2 (Smith, Lhakpa and Tshering Sherpa made cache). About a week later summit push from ABC by Bishop, Smith, Lhakpa and Tshering to C2 and on to C3 (Chuntz had left expedition as summit party started up due to intestinal problems). Left C3; at 7200m Bishop and Lhakpa (because Bishop too slow and had bad cough) turned back; left oxygen at cache and went up to 7600m, where found abandoned Italian (W Ridge) tent partly ruined and zippers didn't work. Spent sleepless night and next morning decided didn't have enough strength to go on. Now too late to make another bid before yaks arrived. Also Sherpas had been promised only one summit push by them and Bishop's health not very good.

ABC at bottom of slope on east side of Col
C4  at North Col

ROUTEMEMO:
C4 deposit made by 25th Sept but not occupied before 30th because of acclimatization. 1st Oct summit bid from C4 by Berger, De La Ferriere and Muller. Berger to top, but De La Ferriere was without oxygen and too difficult and Muller returned with her (his wife); all 3 in C4 that night. Hubert arrived at BC very late and tried for summit on 9th Oct from C4 and stopped 8100-8200m because intestinal problem.


Letter to Miss Hawley - 15 Oct 1992
From Berger Eugene

I was member of Bernard Muller's expedition. A first attempt was started from C2 on Sept 26 but because of strong wind we (Bernard Muller, De La Ferriere + Ang Phurba) went back to BC.

After two days of rest we started again on 29 Sept (BC -> C2). 30 Sept (C2 -> C4) we reached C4 at 16 hours approximately.

On 1st of October I started together with Basque climber Jesus Extaniz (?) at 1 hour 30 in the morning. Bernard Muller, De La Ferriere and Ang Phurba started 1/2 hour later.

I had the same ryhme as the Basque climber but in the following I was waiting two times 1 hour (more more?) for my team members who were slowly because Lawrence didn't use oxygen. I had French oxygen but it causes some problems, mask freezing, bottle screw was unfit. Meanwhile the Basque climber went to top (9-10 am) I was waiting at about 8700m (ridge below south summit) the last time for my team members. There we decided that I would continue alone, the others went a little higher but turned back soon. Just below south summit I met Basque climber who came down from summit. I reached south summit at 11:29 am. The final ridge was very steep and unfortunately I damaged my balloon (oxygen) with my ice-axe any many oxygen was going out of the balloon not in my mask but in the air. So the last 100 meters were really hard for me, really the hardest thing I ever did in the mountain. I reached top on 1:45 pm exactly. On the top I saw the Italian "tripod," I took some photos (you find hereby). The Basque flag was also on the "tripod."

After 5-10 minutes I went back. The descent without oxygen from the top was really hard and I could reach south col at 17:30 just before darkness, where I met my team members again.

2 October I went back to BC.
ACCIDENTS: Rouit edema at BC (evacuated by helicopter)

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 7300m due to sickness of member
ROUTEMEMO:
BC at Iman Gurung arrived at BC - Mani Lal Gurung and Nuru Thapa made.

Had been on Xixapangma with French expedition immediately before going to Everest, spent 4 nights in KTM (2 of them waiting for Lukla flight). When Iman arrived at BC, Mani Lal Gurung (from some village in Gorkha district called Lhaprak) had made C2 about a week before and put there food and cooking supplies. Iman started up from BC at 5 pm 7th reached C3 at 10:45 pm on 7th - had caught cold on 5th and had slight fever; at 6500m and very difficult with running nose and sore throat and painful coughing. Stopped at C3 7300m 20 minutes and then down (with Mani Lal from C2) and arrived BC 3 am. 7th was good moonlight and good time for summit bid. Stayed BC 2 days only with fever and coughing so left mountain. Iman never slept in C2 or any other above BC.

Iman paid for 2 HA men and 3 BC staff; $1000 royalty (10% of normal) and shared salary of Ukranians' liaison officier and funds from French.
 
Wants to try speed climb again but not to pay so much, so go with others expedition.

2nd HA man=Nun Thapa who went to BC, got sick, went to Pheriche and died there.
ACCIDENTS: Iman Gurung sick (flu?)

ROUTEMEMO:
1st summit bid was by Pasang Lhamu (with Babu Tshering, Sange) on 25th.

2nd bid by her again with her 3 Sherpas plus Vincent, Arvis & Maurus, Powers & Sesma on 26th; Pasang's party reached 8400m and French to 8400m and all back because of wind. 

3rd summit bid on 3rd Oct by Vincent for half an hour, had trouble with headlamp & it was windy. 

7th Oct Vincent (alone from C2) left C4 at midnight alone entirely and on top at 9:30 am (slow beause tired) and down to Col for the night. 

5th bid on 9th by Darsney only from this team; left col 1 am and on top after 11 hrs (also tired).

Pasang Lhamu had an entirely separate party: her own tents, food, oxygen, etc and her own team of 3 climbing Sherpas, plus her husband Sonam in support to C2. All of these climbers also used oxgyen at and above South Col. She left mountain after her attempts 25th and 26th because tired (and according to her brother-in-Law, because Sonam had to return to his trekking business in Kathmandu).
ACCIDENTS: 1 member serious altitude sickness; nothing else

ROUTEMEMO:
1st summit bid planned for 4th Oct by 2 members who 1st occupied C4, but they didn't leave tent that day because of wind and on 5th were now too tired and down. 

Next summit party arrived at C4 on 8th and up the 9th except Johnson, who did not feel like going up. Delean went to 8300m & Brad Bull to 8700m and gave up because Delean tired and Bull too slow; Tashi stayed with Bull, so also did not summit. All others from C4 reached top as follows: Pasang Kazi 7:30 am; De La Parro 7:35; Apa (his 4th ascent) 8:00 & Berg with him; Ortega 9 am. No other summit bids.

Fitch Watkins and Hoffman (his loyal client) hatched the plan to climb Everest as one of the Hoffman's 7 summits and got the permit in 1990 and Fitch Watkins hired Berg to guide the mountain; Ortega was also hired to guide climbing through never on Everest before. $17,000 each paid by all members except Fitch Watkins, Berg and Ortega. When team got to BC, it turned out promised supplies included only 6 climbing Sherpas (instead of 9), small BC staff and facilities, fewer oxygen bottles, etc (Fitch Watkins had built new house); Fitch Watkins was confronted by team late Sept when team should have been summiting but came down to BC for confrontation. Sergio was at BC because didn't like to go through Icefall; confrontation one afternoon and he disappeared from BC at 6:00 am, leaving with Elias who was tired and homesick.
ACCIDENTS: Pasang Kazi fell below summit for 200m, self-arrested, broke ribs only

ROUTEMEMO:
25th Sept 10 people from 3 expeditions reached S Summit (22 left S Col from 3 expeditions) and 5 of the 10 got frostbite or other dangers (eye and knee). This was this expedition's 1st summit bid by 7 members, Nima Temba & Dawa Tashi and all reached at best 8400m before turning back. Dacher not well, Djumovits reacting badly to anti-frostbite drug, strong wind, waiting for very slow Spanish to fix ropes to and up Hillary Step.

27th 3 members & Sonam Tshering intended to leave C4 but too much wind and down that day.

3rd Oct attempt planned by Dujmovits, Etschmayer, Pinn, Ratteit, Reichen, Respondek, Treibel, Dawa Tashi & Sonam Tshering from C4 but not above C4 on 3rd and slept in C4. On 4th all down except Djumovits and Sonam Tshering who went to top.

Last people hoping for another summit bid gave up on 6th because of weather.


Ministry of Tourism - 8 Oct 1992

Dujmovits and Sonam Tshering on 4 Oct left Col 2:45, on top 9:07 am in bad weather, on 25 minutes on top, 4:30 pm at C2.

Sonam's 4th ascent Everest; Dacher to 8400m without oxygen.


Letter to Miss Hawley - 8 Oct 1992 from Ralf Dujmovits

After having seen the 25th of Sept already up to 8500m without oxygen I spent some rest days in BC. (My stomach had not accepted a "Adalai", our doctor gave me at 8400m for a frozen food too).

The 2nd of October me and some of my members went up again to C2 (6500m). The 3rd about twenty French and Spanish and three of my members climbed from C3 to South Col. Also me and two of my group climbed from C2 to South Col. On arrival it was already very windy, so spent a horrible stormy night (without oxygen). Only three Spanish Juan Thomas, Pedro Jose Tous and Mikel Reparez started and reached later the summit.

We spent the whole day on South Col (using from time to time oxygen). The next stormy night started. At 2:45 together with Sonam Tshering, our Sirdar (3 times summit), I started from South Col. It was still more stormy than the night before, but less cold (-24 degree C). After 2-1/2 hours we reached the South East Ridge by changing the guide role steadily. At 8:00 reached the South Summit, Sonam 10 minutes later. It was terribly stormy. 500m long "snow-flags" were blown from ridge into the sky.

9:00 clock me and 10 minutes later Sonam reached the summit. From the new Italian and Tsering Tripole/ took off a Sashe flag. I took some pictures of Sonam and summit. Sonam of me also.

At 12:30 after a difficult descent in the incoming storm we were bad in South Col, at 1600 o'clock in C2.

After my calculation after 13 years I was the 14th German on summit. The 13th German was Schmatz. For Sonam Tshering, it was the fourth climb to summit of Everest.

All other climbers of my team have abandoned their attempts and we finished the expedition.

Yesterday at 9:30 Michel Vincent, leader of French-International expedition, had reached summit alone. Up to now (8 Oct, 6:30 am, -12 degrees inside but cold fingers for writing) we have received no other, no more information about him.
ACCIDENTS: None

ROUTEMEMO:
C2 slightly lower than most others
C3 on Lhotse Face
C4 at South Col.

Stayed a few days at Pyramid's at Lobuche (5050m) for physiological tests and then to BC. We went upwards to S Col, "fixed the rope" and put deposit at col on 22nd but slept there on 27th only. On 28th 1st attempt with 4 Sherpas and 7 members with more than 15 kg of scientific work (altitude measurements) of tripod, satellite recorder, etc. Left col at 3:30 am ("too late") and of these S Summit reached by 3 Sherpas and 5 members. Two Sherpas ran out of oxygen at that altitude [and Chamoux without oxygen] turned back because of getting late. 4 members and 1 Sherpa on top at 2 pm and back to C4. 29th Chamoux with Santin left S Col and reached top, taking along equipment left by others at S Summit, left C3 at 3 am and on top 10 am; spent more than 2 hrs fixing equipment and contacting Chinese in Tibet and Italians at Lobuche and they beamed light from Tibet and laser from Nepal, contacting satellite, etc. to measure altitude. 30th Blanc and Vesga left Col and on top.

Had to pay 2nd royalty to change route from S Pillar.
ACCIDENTS: Moro cerebral edema 7600m on Sep 22

ROUTEMEMO:
1st summit attempt on 25th Sept by 2 members who reached S Summit and stopped by wind. 2nd bid from col 27th aborted by wind, except Tardivel who went up alone & stopped at S Summit to C2 in 4-5 hrs, skiing below col between S Pillar & Genveva Spur. 3rd bid on 3rd Oct when stayed 2 nights at col; on 4th 2 members reached 8100m & quit because of wind. 9th Oct finally had success; 1 member without oxygen reached 8600m, realized he was too slow & gave up.


Batard - 8 Oct 92

Batard arrived 12 Sept BC and started up on 16 Sept to C2. 17 & 18 Sept C2. 19th to C3 and down to BC to rest (C4 already there; stayed 15 mins). In BC 20-23rd to C2, 24th to C3. 25th to 7500m, then down because saw summiters going very slowly and not now good and (on this down Pasang deposited supplies at South Summit); Batard BC. 28th 5:00 am from BC and in 10 hours at Col but many clouds so stopped at Col. 29th started up at 5:30 am but "was not so well in my head" because believed wind starting when it in fact was not windy. Reached 8300m quickly but then felt cold and returned to C4 to sleep and at noon down to Lobuche to meet Bruno and Jean-Michel. Stayed at Lobuche 2 days and on 1st Oct to C2. 2nd Oct reached Col and really strong wind; slept at Col. Now on 3rd Batard and Asselin and Gallet amongst 40 people at Col; only Spanish took a risk and went to top while Batard and 2 French to BC: climb finished for them because tired "and Oct is the time for wind" - this was enough. To sleep on summit, Batard needed good weather. Had now abandoned Everest and wants to do difficult technical route alone on South Face Nuptse.


Batard - 1 Sept 92

I want to be the 1st man to sleep in highest point on earth. Medical experts say dangerous to sleep there without oxygen but Batard says: "No, it is not dangerous for me." Danger is on top early because Asselin and Gallet take pix of him there and then they descend - arrive top 3:00-4:00 pm and then Asselin and Gallet to South Col to wait for Batard. Best time to try for top is full moon time (11 Oct).

Not to compete with Iman Singh Gurung in his bid to scale Everest in 20 hours unless Gallet and Asselin are sick and cannot ascend with Batard, in which case Batard perhaps goes up quickly.

Iman can succeed in 20 hours if gets good acclimatization but not because exhausted on Xixa.

Return KTM as soon as possible.
ACCIDENTS: Jacquet pneumonia; Aubertin great pain in knees; Ang Gyalzen fell into river after leaving BC for home village

SPONSOR: 3 Spanish Groups of Friends to Everest
ROUTEMEMO:
C4 at South Col.

On 25th 4 summiters and Ang Rita left C4 1:30 am and reached S Summit 12:00 in little wind; had to open the way in not very deep snow as first to try for summit. 28 people left C4, but only 8 members of all expeditions and 2 Sherpas reached S Summit (Pasang Lhamu was in group of 28 and reached only 8300-8400m). Ang Rita turned back at S Summit because of wind and Hillary Step dangerous. 2 French reached Hillary Step and only 4 people to top, which reached at 3 pm in strong wind, but could stand up - found nothing on top. Was clear weather at high altitudes. Returned to C4 at 8 pm. Descending on 26th Felix could not see at all well.

Bereziartua arrived BC 26th Sept from Cho Oyu. Left S Col 2 am with 2 French, including woman, 1 French Sherpa and 1 Lux, but 1 went faster and top reached 8:50 am (at time Lux arrived S Summit). Lux on top 10:00+ am; French and their Sherpa 8600m only.

* order on top: 
  25 Set - Eguillor and Fernandez; Alberto and Felix Inurrategi 10 minutes later.
   1 Oct - Bereziartua at 8:50 am; Luxembourger from Muller expedition 1:00 pm.
   3 Oct - Tomas, Reparaz and Tous together at 12:10 pm


Tous - 12 Oct:

Ang Rita used oxygen in night of 24th in C4 because had stomach trouble, but did not use next day above C4. On 25th did not want to go to top, but was told by Spaniard you are Sherpa and he tried for top, but stopped at South Summit.


Egusiktza - 28 Sept

Pixti and Fernandez badly frostbitten toes and F pneumonia also - by helicopter to KTM today.

Very late on Friday - Ang Rita back at South top not on summit; brothers without oxygen and others with oxygen on top 3:10 pm; brothers quickly down others slowly and at 8700m biv at 6:00 pm and down next am to Col. Juan Tomas doctor diagnosed pneumonia. All to BC Sunday.

Brothers to South Col after dark Friday; Alberto tripped there and pulled knee ligament.
ACCIDENTS: Felix retinal hemorrhage? from day after summit; 2 members frostbitten toes and fingers (hospitalized in Spain)

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 8750m due to winds and cold (even at BC)
ROUTEMEMO:
C2 in Western Cwm
C3 on SW Face (same as Bonington)
C4 on SW Face (same as Japanese)
C5 on SW Face (start of Bonington couloir)
C6 on SW Face above rock band (same as Bonington and Japanese 1991).

After C4 established, fixed ropes directly towards top to make new route. Reached 8000m at bottom of rock band, then down to consider situation. Considering lack of good acclimatization, no Sherpas to carry loads, would too long to open new route so decided on 7th Oct to abandon plans for new route and following Bonington route. 18th Oct Gonchar, Pastukh & Svergun reached 8500m; Gonchar got frostbite fingers and Pastukh infection and down to C2 while Svergun stayed at C4. 19th Oct Svergun to S Summit in dark with no watch and headlamp batteries dead; waited for moon to rise but was time of new moon at place where he found ropes but where he was doesn't know. Started freezing in very cold night; very dark night and very steep wall, but he had no new ropes of his own. Then after 3-4 hrs wait very strong wind came up and he decided to descend and reached C4 at 4 am. Now he couldn't breathe (pul. edema?) and found very big oxygen bottle, took oxygen from it without gear, descended with it on rope, taking oxygen from it occasionally and reached C4 20th about noon. Left C4 and again down that aft/eve and arrived at C2 4 am of 21st again with his oxygen bottle sliding before him, helping him to avoid crevasse as well as continuing to supplying occasional oxygen and on 21st afternoon left C2 and arrived at BC at 9 am. Had used expedition's own oxygen and mask in C2 and to BC with others. When arrived at BC doctor heard lungs and thought now pneumonia and spent that night oxygen at BC.

Pelle's expedition had left tent and supplies at S Col and thought Svergun might go to col. Turkevich and Obichod had gone to this col camp for 2 nights in worst wind. Turkevich had even seen and been in broken tent. Made no attempt on summit because winds made this impossible.

2 more attempts for top via face but both stopped by winds at C4 on 21 & 24th; finally on 25th brought down C4 & C3 gear.

Profit - Lhotse S Face more difficult than Everest SW Face by Bonington route; but if making direct route up Everest face to summit, forcing rock band 6400m high then Everest SW Face more difficult.
             
Profit - 5 Nov 92: Svergun still says he doesn't know his highest point. There was a big wall and a number of fixed ropes, but it was a dark night and he confused by lack of oxygen. It is not possible to climb in the S Summit gully and is necessary to climb to left or right of it. Perhaps he went to left and behind S Summit.
ACCIDENTS: Some minor frostbite, edema/pneumonia

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 7750m due to lack of strength and of time
ROUTEMEMO:
Garrido went into icefall 20th Dec to see how route was but was very weak from too fast trek to BC (4 days from KTM/Lukla to BC) and did not reach C1. Went to Pheriche 26th Dec to recover while Iman Gurung, Ang Tshering and Ang Nima repaired icefall route and returned to BC 3-4 Jan. Then 1 week some snowfall, foggy, wind. 15th Jan all 4 men up from BC to make camp at 6500m at normal C2 site with one tent and all loads. Garrido 1-1/2 hours behind 3 Nepalis, who would pitch camp and return to BC while Garrido climbed. But Ang Tshering going fast through icefall even in dangerous places; at 6300m he fell into crevasse slightly hidden by snow (but there were British fixed ropes, but he didn't belay). He fell 150m in crevasse and couldn't be seen and too dangerous to descend into it because of ice overhangs; all survivors to BC. 

Garrido waited for Ang Tshering relative to come and also to engage another Sherpa to help remove all British equipment at the end. 26th Jan 4 men again up, but route in bad condition and took long time to get through icefall; reached C2 site on 27th and 3 Nepalis down to BC. Garrido went to C3 site 1 Feb, tried for S Col but got only to 7750-7800m, above yellow band and bived there in bad night because placed tent badly; stopped here because not strong enough to go higher. 4 Feb very cloudy and snowfall and decided to go down. These days very cold but not very windy. 4th down to C2. 5th terrible windy day - couldn't move, 6th good weather but arrived not strong enough to go up and decided he needed a week in BC to get stronger and down to BC on 6th. Then decided to give up: too short time left to recover and try again.

Would like to do solo from north side with no icefall problems. Want to go next winter if Tibet Mountain Assn gives permit. Likes winter with snow very hard and perfect to walk and a little more difficult and more exciting "with no one else around."

Garrido arrived BC 18 Dec and British left icefall equipment for him (for $4000). Reported to have been sick and gone to Pheriche to recover until early in Jan.


Neame - 5 Jan 1993

Handed over by British: icefall route, ladders in Cwm, tent at C3 and ropes to South Col and 3 Sherpas maintaining Icefall.

Garrido had chest problem but probably at BC or above by now, He said he was prepared to wait until mid-Feb.
ACCIDENTS: Garrido slight pulmonary edema going to BC too fast

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 7900m due to effects of storm
ROUTEMEMO:
C1 at top of Icefall
C2 in Western Cwm
C3 on Lhotse Face
High point at South Col.

Icefall in "horrific" condition with route not having been maintained as promised. Argued with Asian Trekking about this and about the sirdar, Ang Tshering of Khumbu, "unreliable," a drunkard, and the Sherpa team who were "yak herders" (Asian Tkg. agrees sirdar's wages not to be paid) and who once rested throwing rocks at each other (Pangboche men vs Khumjung men). 

Icefall very unstable especially at top end, much more so than in spring 1976 when Neame was on Everest and "took its toll on people's nerves." Above 7300m totally different wind conditions from those below. Had cursory look at S Pillar, but early on hoped to beat the winds (jet stream) with push on normal route, which had more ropes left from autumn rather than fixing pillar, where no ropes to be seen and no platform ledges also. Route to C3 appeared on 28th Nov but not occupied until next day by Harry Taylor alone after Sherpa turned back 150 ft below camp site because it was cold and windy (Sherpas given same clothing as members). Now in early Dec, a period of high winds to 9th Dec, during which stocked C2 and C3. Weather forecast that 9th and then on 13th would be good; 9th wasn't. C3 occupied on 12th but now forecast unfavorable and down again (skeleton crew at C2 and others to BC). Forecast next for 19th (on which date Sherpas fixed route to col with Mike Smith below them a bit; some of route already fixed well) and Smith spent 8 nights/9 days continuously at C2, 3 nights alone. Sherpas ignored instructions, on 20th dumped oxygen at yellow band instead of col and descended to C2 instead of C3 only. 

Now Sherpas made a nonsense of logistical plans. 23rd forecast to be good. On 21st Smith joined in light snow showers by Taylor, Tinker, Duff and Pelkey in C3. 22nd 4 members planned to move to C4 and Sherpas to carry loads to C4 but no Sherpas moved out of C2 that day because slight mist. With forecast that jet stream would sit overhead from 25th indefinitely, light push on 22nd seen at last chance and was made by Taylor, Smith, Pelkey and Duff from C3, picking up oxygen at yellow band with biv at col and Taylor and Pelkey to top on 23rd. On 22nd, 4 set off for col at 11 am (late to minimize hours at col and C3 very cold till sun reached it at 10:30 am), Pelkey slipped on fixed ropes at yellow band in fresh snow on top of ice and ripped shoulder muscles, all 4 going very slowly with heavy loads, fresh snow underfoot and worsening weather so at 4:15 pm gave it up at 7900m because facing "an epic at the col" (Smith) in wind and snow, were going slowly, due to Pelkey's shoulder, Duff unwell from believed onset of cerebral edema and toes freezing (other 2 OK). Slept in C3 but Pelkey on verge of hypothermia and had to put up another tent which took long time. 

Then storm worsened that night: 
  C3 - 1 of 2 tents destroyed 

On 23rd and 23rd/24th night:
  C2 - 6 of 9 tents destroyed and 2 destroyed but usable
  C1 - 2 of 2 tents destroyed

BC - really untouched

All in BC 24th except Neve. Descent from C3 to C2 had been an epic in itself. In cwm 120 mph gusts on 23rd and temperature below -30 degrees centigrade day time and night, "flesh-freezing kind of cold" (Smith whose cheeks had sunface frostbite).

25th morning meeting decided no more attempts: "weather forecasts" for next week at least (Jan no success in past), damaged camps would have had to be rebuilt, "useless Sherpas" and "state of team" with few potential summits in tents of experience and remaining strength (only Neve and Neame still fit and experienced) so "what was point of continuing, acclimatizing risk with little chance of success?" Smith: "I think we should have gone back" after several weeks" rest.
ACCIDENTS: 2 Sherpas injured in icefall (1 broken leg, 1 broken ribs and 'banged' head)

ROUTEMEMO:
C1 at top of Icefall
C2 in Western Cwm
C3 on Lhotse Face
C4 at Col.

Took 1 hr to trek past all C2 camps to this team's C2. This season Koreans (SW Face) charged $200 per foreigner to go through icefall. Tried to make 1st summit bid for 10 May but Pujante hit by block of ice on 9th May while going up between C3 and C4 and Pujante's head cut open and bled profusely and he was brought down to C2 where US doctor (Rabold) sewed wound. Then waited for good weather forecast from British satellite system; very windy from 11th to 15th. C4 reached 15th by Ang Phurba and Pujante (now recovered) and 16th May left C4 midnight, and summited at 10:40 am and C4 at 3 pm and C2 at 7 pm. Pujante and Ang Phurba used oxygen from C4 up because Pujante plans to climb all seven summits and all 8000ers and wanted to be sure to succeed. 

Also on 16th 10 pm 4 people started up from col: Blade, Cadiach, De la Matta and Rafols with no Sherpas and no oxygen ever. At 8300m+ Blade and Rafols too slow (had reached col on 16th at 7 pm and were too tired) turned back at midnight or 1 am. 17th May De la Matta at S Summit 2 pm, did not feel able to reach top and returned to col same day; arrived at S Summit with Cadiach who went on alone to top at 3:30 pm alone and back to col 8 pm on headlamp safely and without frostbite. 

Others at col wanted to try top on 18th again without oxygen and too windy so down at 3 pm.

Cleaning: BC area much cleaner than in 1982, but Catalans Sherpas cleared away rubbish which they carried to Lobuche.
ACCIDENTS: Pujante hit by ice block but not serious

ROUTEMEMO:
C1 at top of Icefall
C2 in Western Cwm 
C3 on Lhotse Face

During the next 10 days, the group, consisting of climbers, trekkers, Sherpas, porters and yaks trekked upward toward Everest Base Camp. The trek passed through the mountain villages of Phakding, Jorsale, Namche Bazaar, Tengboche, Pheriche, Dingboche, Lobuche and Gorak Shep. Everyone was picking litter on the trail and carrying it to the next camp; carrying the extra weight was difficult with the altitude, but the result - cleaner trail - made it worth the challenge.

On April 13th the group, in reasonably good health and excellent spirits, arrived in BC. 
On the following day, the puja ceremony was performed, a traditional Buddist blessing of the climbers and the expedition. It was an especially auspicious day to hold a puja because the weather was clear and calm - a good omen. Armed with trash bags, the entire group swept the Base Camp area for trash, where they collected 60 kilos of trash left from previous expeditions. 

During the next  week, eight of the ten members made carries through the icefall to C1. Then, C2 was established and was occupied by the eight members. The team and Sherpas would now begin to make carries to C3. Each day the team would start the climb in the cold and darkness of early morning when the icefall was more stable with less chance of collapse or avalanche. 
A few days later Guy ventured through the icefall where he stayed at C1.

Meanwhile, Tommy now recovered began making his way up the mountain. By April 30th, Americans on Sagarmatha continued to be ahead of schedule. Tommy and Guy, now together, moved up to C2 getting accimatized, while the rest of the team headed back to BC for rest and recuperation after seven days at higher altitudes.

Over the past weeks, the rest of the team had established three camps while carrying numerous loads of supplies and equipment up the mountain. The South Col route, had been climbed four times as the high altitude camps were established.

Big avalanche from Changtse & another big one from N Col on 14th were expecially alarming. Body cremated at old Rongbuk 13th. LO said team could go to other route or some to join other teams, but no one wanted to continue & advice from sponsors was to stop in such dangerous conditions. But Everest was Stronger - by Jon Gangdal
(Received from Gangal - 14 March 1995)

"We have had an accident. A major avalanche has swept right over us. Four Sherpas were taken by the avalanche, and a fifth has lost one of his fingers."

The message came clear and slowly over the radio from C2 at 6600m. It could not be mistaken. Everything had seemed so perfect, the expedition was experiencing great progress on the mountain, but everything had turned upside down within seconds and a major tragedy had happened. Mingma Norbu Sherpa was shortly found dead in the avalanche at the bottom of the mountain, 700m further down from C2. He left behind a pregnant women and two children, two years and five years old.

We had set us a very ambitious goal. The West Ridge on Mount Everest (8848m) from Tibet. One of the by far hardest and toughest routes on the worlds highest mountain. The route had been attempted by a dozen earlier expeditions. Only one had succeeded. That was during the spring. We were going to try the route during the autumn, and thereby write another proud chapter in Norwegian Himalaya history.

We knew very well that our attempt could be very dangerous, like all climbing in the Himalayas. For that reason we had gone through 3 years of very thorough preparations and taken as many precautions as humans can take. This had made the Norwegian Everest Expedition to Norway's largest climbing expedition ever, with 22 Norwegian climbers - 20 men and 2 women, 15 Sherpas and close to 10 tons of food and equipment.

Ahead of Schedule

When the accident and tragedy struck the expedition, the expedition had reached every goal up to that point. We were considerably ahead of schedule, thanks to two very strong teams who had during the course of less than one week, managed to fix ropes and carry equipment above the first magic point of 7000m. At the same time a dozen Norwegians and Sherpas were working on carrying food and equipment from Advance Base Camp (5600m) up to C1 at 5900m, which were located by the foot of the mountain.

24 hours of continous snowfall put a temporary stop on the record breaking progress. At that time all the climbers who were evaluated to be in good enough form had spent a least one night in C2 at 6600m. The few who were still fighting the after effects from high altitude sickness, flue and colds, were on their way to full recovery. The team was doing very well.

After some discussion we had reached an agreement regarding progress on the mountain. The climbers literally queued up in order to help out on the mountain. Even the most pessimistic climbers started to believe that we would reach the summit.

A Beautiful Day

The third day after the snowfall, Monday Sept 12th was a cold beautiful day. Three Norwegians and six Sherpas were on the ropes before 8 am and made good progress towards C2, even though they had to plow their way at times in knee-deep snow. But even though the snow was deep in certain places, it appeared solid and not very likely to start any avalanches.

The plan was to reach 7350m that afternoon and establish C3 on the top of the West Shoulder. The Norwegians and two Sherpas were to stay there overnight and to stretch climing ropes along the west ridge the following day. The four other Sherpas were going to return to C1.

It were these four Sherpas who started climbing from C2 after a short break with juice and chocolate. Three of the Sherpas were tied to the ropes. The fourth was a short distance behind and was just about to tie himself on the to the ropes when a major roar suddenly interrupted the silence on the mountain and massive amounts of snow thundered towards the climber.

The ones who were still in C2 saw that the avalanche had started far to the left of the Sherpas. For a moment they hoped that the snow would avoid the four Sherpas. This did not happen. They last they could see was a chaos of snow, arms and legs rushing past the point where they were staying. The avalanche also swept over the ones who were still in the C2. Luckily they managed to hold on to the ropes.

Despiration

The complete silence which always follows immediately after huge avalanches was very brief. The Sherpas very quickly became aware of what happened and cried and yelled in desperation over the fact that they had lost one of their closest friends and family member.

We found Mingma under only 20 cm of snow. He was probably killed instantly during the fall down the 700m high mountain side. Thanks to his very strong Sherpa friends we were able to carry him all the way down to BC the following day.

While the rescue work continued on the mountain, relatives, sponsors and media in Norway were informed through our satellite telephone. Mingma's relatives in Kathmandu were informed. The only ones who didn't get any information before one week after the avalanche were Mingma's pregnant wife and two children. This is the time it took Mingma's brother to travel from Base Camp to Mingma's hometown Rolwaling which is four days by foot from Kathmandu.

At that time a husband and father to two beautiful daughters had been ashes for six days. The day after the avalanche Mingma was according to Buddhist customs cremated in a monastery a couple of kms below BC.

Postpone or continue the expedition?

Before our departure from Norway we had discussed what we should do in the situation where someone died on the mountain. Nobody had been able to give an unambiguous answer. The most important elements with such discussions is not to draw the most substantial conclusions but rather be able to think through unpleasant and frightening approaches. This is one of the critical elements in the mental preparations to risky projects. We decided to divide the discussions in two faces. First it was important to evaluate all sides with the accident. Then we waited for one day, in order to reach a conclusion of postponing or continuing the expedition. There were mixed reactions. Nobody wanted to continue on the West Ridge, but about 50% of the climbers wanted to explore the possibility of climbing other routes on Everest, or other adjacent mountains. The rest wanted to postpone the expedition and go home. As a climber I wanted to continue along another route. As the expeditions leader I concluded differently.

"Our common goal was to climb Everest along the West Ridge. We can choose another route and in many ways reach our goal. But based on the worsening conditions we have concluded that this could above be very dangerous. We cannot afford yet another accident. To let someone climb another and lower mountain is too far away from our original goal, and will therefore not add any additional value to the expedition. In many ways it would be the opposite, it would split the expedition. We left Norway as a team, and should therefore return as a team. I have therefore decided to postpone the expedition at this time and go home.

Four days later the whole Lhotse Face came down in one enormous avalanche. It happened in the middle of the night, at 00:30 am and the avalanche was so strong that people woke up in their tents because of the air pressure reaching Base Camp, 17 kilometers away.

The day before one climber almost was hit by an avalanche coming down the West Face of Changtse.

After this, we did not regret to much our decision fo postponing the expedition.
ACCIDENTS: Ang Temba's finger end cut off by taut rope at time 4 others were hit by avalanche; Mingma Norbu killed by avalanche

C1 at bottom of North Face
C2 on North Face well southwest of Great Col
High point at North Face.

C1 in Icefall
C2 in Western Cwm

High point at South Col.

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 8300m due to winds
ROUTEMEMO:
4 climbing members reached only 7900m on 23 Sept. Only Sherpas went higher fixing rope to 8300m.

Sports Activities :

The Camp Base was installed at 5200m on the 4th of September.

The 13th of September the ABC was installed. C1 was installed at 7050m at the north Col, on 17th of Sept.

The C2 was installed on the 23rd of Sept at 7800m on the North NE Ridge.

On the next days fixed ropes was fixed on the ridge onto 8300m. Been impossible to install C3 due to the strong wind at this altitude, the expedition was forced down to ABC.

Due to changing weather conditions (windy and stormy) and that the autumn came before its time, the members [saw it ]was impossible to press higher than 7400m, then the expedition made the decision to retire from the mountain.

The 4th of Oct with a little change in the weather conditions, 4 members of the team and sirdar Dorje Sherpa, climbed the Lhakpa Peak (7045m) located northeast of Everest. The 10th of Oct, the team left the ABC and the 15th the team left the BC, arriving in Kathmandu on the 18th of October.

Scientific Activities:

During the expedition, the team had collected (picked up), geological samples, Botanic samples and Water samples (from the different Glacier Rivers) for its study and analysis in differents institutes of the CSICC.

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 8300m due to strong cold winds
ROUTEMEMO:
C1 at North Col
C2 at North Ridge
C3 at North Face
High point at North Face.

4 and 9 Oct parties tried to go to summit but no success. 9th Oct 9 people to C2 and 10th 4 of them slept in C3. 11th no communication with 4-man party and 2 from below tried to meet them but very strong wind at 7500m to 8000m. The 4 stayed 2 nights in C2, moving it to 8300m. 13th communication established and highest team advised to come down as temperature had suddenly dropped and winds continued and slowly party descended to North Col as dark was falling and 14th to ABC. 15th yaks arrived BC. 

10 strong climbers and plenty of supplies but winds and cold.
ACCIDENTS: Krivocheev slight frostbite; Efimov had no strength from cold or what?

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 8300m due to cold wind & bad weather
ROUTEMEMO:
High point on SE Ridge.

Summit attempt from BC at 4:00 pm 10 Oct arrive C4 1:00 am 11 Oct and 400m above Col and then "many winds" at 7:00 am and turned back and descended to BC same day. 2 teammates sent up with supplies to C4 on 28 Sept but one got frostbite at C3 on 29th so they down to BC and which reached BC 3 Oct and helicoptered to KTM. Mingma again up to Col on 10 Oct before Kaji. Mingma had not left at C3 as requested Kaji's climbing suit so Kaji arrived at Col only in cotton shirt (though had enough energy to climb and through night to C3 without climbing suit - arrived C3 at 9:30 pm). Climbing suit was at Col and put it on and got into sleeping bag for an hour to get warm. Main reason for failure was his being cold as he did not wear climbing suit from BC because it weighs 1 kg.

Wants to try again next spring.

Japanese Nukita said 20 Oct that Nepalese used other people's tents.
ACCIDENTS: Lhakpa frostbitten toes & fingers all black

SPONSOR: Group on UK Medical Everest Expedition permit
TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 7900m due to wind
ROUTEMEMO:
C1 at top of Icefall
C2 in Western Cwm
C3 on Lhotse Face
C4 at South Col.

"There were 2-3 days of no wind but in these days we were not in the right place, maybe we make a mistake not to try before 1st Oct, but we didn't have oxygen at S Col." Weather was very fine in late Sept.

1st night slept at South Col was 11 Oct (La Ferriere, Hubert, Muller, Pacheco and Renard and 4 Sherpas (Sonam Dendu, Nawang Pura/Phura, 2 others)). During night of 11th tent broken by wind and no one went above Col but all descended to C2 and climb finished.
ACCIDENTS: Nothing

TERMNOTE: Abandoned at 8200m due to winds
ROUTEMEMO:
BC at road
C1 at North Col
C2 on North Ridge
C3 on North Ridge.

Winds started 30th Sept. On 27th Kawalzik & Guarachi tried to go to top from ABC, which left 9 am, reached C2 5 pm, stayed 4-1/2 hours & 9:30 pm left C2 to go to top, reached 8050m & returned (Kowalzik too cold & Guarachi feared too deep snow for a person to climb alone) back to C2 1 am 28th. 

28th 10:00 am same 2 members & 4 Sherpas left C2 again pitched C3 but all except Guarachi down to ABC & no one in C2. Guarachi now wanted to attempt summit alone but next morning decided to descend because didn't like avalanching on N Face's middle where 1 km wide avalanche down on 30th. 

No one ever again reached C3 & only Kowalzik, Guarachi & 3 Sherpas reached C2 on 10th Oct. Winds so strong couldn't move without using fixed ropes from N Col up.

4 members left expedition on 2 Oct: 1 was sick, others no longer motivated?
